questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What bronze's alloying contributes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how adding tin changes the working properties of copper
questions.stem: A field survey team records a bronze marker plate that is harder than a pure copper sheet of equal thickness. Why does the alloying change this property?

options.text: Tin added to copper forms a harder alloy, so the marker resists denting and abrasion in the field
Tin makes the metal lighter than pure copper, so the marker weighs less than its size suggests
options.misconception: treats the added tin as making the alloy lighter

options.text: Tin prevents corrosion entirely, so the marker can stay outdoors without any treatment
options.misconception: assumes tin makes the alloy corrosion proof

options.text: Tin lowers the melting point, so the alloy can be poured at a lower heat than copper alone
options.misconception: believes the alloy pours at a much lower temperature

questions.explanation: Bronze is copper with some tin, and the alloy's rigid crystal structure makes it harder and more wear resistant than pure copper. It is no lighter and still corrodes, so those claims fail.
questions.hint: Ask what the second metal does to the crystal structure.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What produces the colour of a patina
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a two tone patina as evidence of local conditions
questions.stem: Along a transect, photographs show a bronze survey pin that is green in damp soil and dark brown where rain and air reach it. What does the pattern indicate?

options.text: That the two sections were made from different alloys, one bronze and one painted steel marker
options.misconception: reads the two colours as different materials

options.text: That copper compounds form with moisture and oxygen, and different conditions give differently coloured films
That the green is moss and the brown is rust, so both colours come from plant and iron staining
options.misconception: reads both colours as surface staining rather than corrosion

options.text: That the brown film is thicker because rain washes the green film away faster than it forms
options.misconception: assumes rain selectively removes the green film

questions.explanation: Copper corrodes in stages, each producing a different coloured compound, so the film depends on oxygen, moisture and the soil. Moss and rust would not both appear on one bronze pin.
questions.hint: Ask what copper does when it meets air and moisture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural logic of a welded sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Compare the structural behaviour of welded and cast sculpture
questions.stem: The expedition asks why a welded steel armature can be built rod by rod while a cast bronze figure must be hollow. Explain the structural difference between the two.

answer.exemplar: A welded armature carries its loads through a frame of members joined to one another, and the maker can place a joint wherever the form needs support, so the structure is assembled from the outside in. A cast figure has no such freedom: a solid pour would trap gas and shrink unevenly, so the sculptor must hollow the form and let it be cast as a shell with the interior removed afterwards.

questions.explanation: Welding joins members freely and lets loads travel along chosen paths, so the form stays open. Casting must enclose a void to avoid gas and shrinkage faults, so mass is defined by a shell.
questions.hint: Ask how each method holds the material together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a kinetic construction different in kind
questions.learningObjective: Explain what distinguishes a kinetic work from a fixed sculpture

stimulus.body: The site log describes a metal armature whose panels turn slowly with the wind. Movement comes from air acting on the unbalanced assembly, no motor is fitted, and the work has no single settled appearance.

questions.stem: The log records a wind driven assembly with no settled appearance. Why is such a work said to differ in kind from a fixed sculpture?

options.text: Because the wind is the artist, so the sculpture cannot be said to have an author or a maker
options.misconception: treats wind as the author and removes human making

options.text: Because the panels are metal, so the material itself makes the work kinetic in the first place
options.misconception: believes the material, not the motion, makes it kinetic

options.text: Because its form depends on forces acting at the moment of viewing, so the work is completed by its movement
Because a moving object has no fixed shape, so it does not qualify as sculpture at all
options.misconception: denies that a moving work can be sculpture

questions.explanation: A kinetic work has no single final form; its appearance is completed by the forces acting on it, so each viewing differs. Metal and wind are the means of that change, not the definition of it.
questions.hint: Ask what finishes the work on each viewing.

questions.topic: What a scale model can claim
questions.learningObjective: State what a scale model can properly claim about a full size work
questions.stem: Stage one: a bronze maquette is modelled at one tenth scale for a survey display. Stage two: the maker sets it beside a full size drawing. What can the model properly claim?

options.text: That it records the monument's material qualities, since the model was cast from the same bronze
options.misconception: assumes the model shares the monument's materials

options.text: That it is a faithful reduced copy, since every dimension is divided by exactly the same factor
options.misconception: assumes uniform scaling preserves every property

options.text: That it carries the same presence as the finished monument, since scale changes size but not effect
options.misconception: believes scale leaves presence and effect unchanged

options.text: That it demonstrates the arrangement and proportion of the monument, without standing for its size or weight

questions.explanation: A scale model is a statement about arrangement, proportion and sightlines; what depends on mass and material behaves differently at one tenth size. Scaling measurements does not scale weight.
questions.hint: Ask what the model is evidence about.

questions.topic: Installation and its dependence on site
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish fundamental dependence on site from practical dependence
questions.stem: The report describes an assembly that cannot be moved without losing its point. What makes its dependence on the site fundamental rather than incidental?

options.text: Its components are too fragile to move, so the dependence on place is a practical matter of handling
options.misconception: reduces the dependence to practical fragility

options.text: Its parts and their relationships were chosen for that place, so relocation destroys the arrangement
The materials were gathered from the surrounding ground, so the site supplies the object with substance
options.misconception: reduces the dependence to where the materials came from

options.text: The permissions to display it were granted for that site alone, so the dependence is a legal one
options.misconception: reduces the dependence to a matter of permission

questions.explanation: Site dependence is fundamental when meaning lies in the work relationship to a place, so moving it severs that relationship. Fragility and permissions are practical matters, not the artistic claim.
questions.hint: Ask what the work would lose if it were moved.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What bronze's alloying contributes
questions.learningObjective: Predict the properties of an alloy from an assay result
questions.stem: An alloy assay of a survey marker gives 90 percent copper and 10 percent tin by weight. Compared with a plate of pure copper of the same size, what does the assay predict?

options.text: A plate that resists corrosion completely, since tin forms an unbroken barrier over the metal
options.misconception: claims the alloy is entirely corrosion proof

options.text: A noticeably lighter plate, since tin is much less dense than the copper it replaces
options.misconception: assumes the added metal makes the alloy lighter

options.text: A stronger and harder plate that resists deformation, since tin stiffens the copper crystal structure
A plate that melts at a lower temperature, since the alloy weakens the metallic bonds
options.misconception: believes the alloy lowers the melting point

questions.explanation: Tin at about a tenth hardens and strengthens copper, which is why bronze was used for hardwearing plates. Tin is denser than copper and the alloy is not corrosion proof, so those claims fail.
questions.hint: Ask what tin does to the crystal structure.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What produces the colour of a patina
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the colour of a patina cannot be fixed in advance
questions.stem: A conservator explains why the colour of a weathered bronze cannot be fixed in advance. Explain what the patina's colour depends upon.

answer.exemplar: The patina is not a coating applied by the maker but a set of chemical compounds that form where copper meets moisture, oxygen and whatever else the air or soil provides. Copper reacts in stages and each stage yields a different colour, so a bronze standing in damp soil, in sea air or in dry sunlight will pass through and settle at different colours, and the patina records the environment as much as the maker's intention.

questions.explanation: Patina colour comes from copper reacting with oxygen, moisture and other substances, so it records the environment rather than a choice. It forms in stages, so it cannot be fixed in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what the patina forms from.

questions.hint: Count the joints before multiplying.

options.text: That the objects are valuable mainly as documents and the arrangement has no expressive role
options.misconception: denies the arrangement any expressive role

options.text: That the display has value only because the objects were made by the same named artist
options.misconception: requires a single named maker for an assemblage

options.text: That every object in an assemblage must be altered so the collection reads as one unified work
options.misconception: believes each object must be altered to unify the display

options.text: That the objects keep their own histories and are joined by the maker arrangement, not altered

questions.explanation: Assemblage brings existing objects together and lets the arrangement carry the meaning while each keeps its history. No common author is needed and nothing must be altered.

questions.topic: What makes a kinetic construction different in kind
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a still day reveals about a wind powered work
questions.stem: Stage one: a mobile sculpture on the ridge turns when wind reaches it. Stage two: on a still day the panels do not move. What does the still day reveal about the work?

options.text: That the element is broken and must be repaired before the installation is reopened
options.misconception: reads the stillness as mechanical failure

options.text: That the movement depends on external forces rather than a motor, so the still day removes its energy source
That the work needs a hidden motor to operate properly at all times of the day
options.misconception: invents a hidden motor for the installation

options.text: That the still day proves the work is really a static sculpture in disguise
options.misconception: concludes the work is only apparently kinetic

questions.explanation: Because the energy comes from the wind, a still day removes the input and the work stands still; nothing is damaged and no motor is needed. The stillness is a fact about weather.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes a scale model useful for testing sightlines
questions.stem: A surveyor argues that a scale model can be used to test the sightlines of a proposed monument. What does that use depend on?

options.text: On the model being exhibited publicly so that many people can confirm the sightlines
options.misconception: makes public display a condition of the test

options.text: On the model being built from the same stone as the finished monument would be
options.misconception: requires the same material for a sightline test

options.text: On the model reproducing the arrangement and viewing angles accurately, which is what sightlines depend on
On the model being cast by the artist who would make the full size work
options.misconception: makes the artist a condition of a useful model

questions.explanation: Sightlines are a question of position, proportion and viewing angle, so a model is useful insofar as it reproduces those. Material, exhibition and authorship do not affect the validity of the check.

questions.stem: Two installation plans are compared for the same work: Version A turns it to face an open view and Version B to face a service yard. Visitors pausing were 40 per hour at A and 6 per hour at B. What does this show?

options.misconception: reduces the site's significance to footfall

options.text: That the service yard version is inferior and should be replaced by the view facing version
options.misconception: judges the version by numbers rather than by meaning

options.text: That visitor numbers depend only on the length of the path, not on what the work faces
options.misconception: attributes the counts to path length alone

options.text: That the meaning and reception of the work change with its position, so the site is part of the work itself

questions.explanation: The same work in two positions produces very different encounters, so site is not an external setting but a condition of the work's meaning. Footfall alone does not make a position good.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What bronze's alloying contributes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how alloying shapes the sound of a bell
questions.stem: A bell caster asks why bronze is used for bells rather than hammered from pure copper. Explain what the alloying contributes to the sound.

answer.exemplar: Bell metal is copper with a substantial addition of tin, usually close to a quarter of the alloy. Tin stiffens the copper so the walls of a bell can be thin without buckling, and it changes the way the metal vibrates so that the partials fall into a set of pitches that a listener recognises as one note. The alloy therefore does two jobs at once: it gives the metal the stiffness to ring and it gives the sound its identity.

questions.explanation: Added tin stiffens the copper so thin walls can ring without buckling and shapes the partials so the note is recognisable. Copper alone is too soft for a bell wall and would not hold that tuning.
questions.hint: Ask what the added metal does to the walls.

questions.stem: A bronze sheet loses 0.4 grams per square metre each year in coastal air. For a sheet with 3 square metres of surface, how many grams are lost over 5 years?
questions.explanation: Each square metre loses 0.4 grams a year, so the three square metre sheet loses 1.2 grams a year. Over five years that is 1.2 times 5, which equals 6 grams of metal lost.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural logic of a welded sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a cracked plate in a welded structure

stimulus.body: A steel plate sculpture in the collection shows cracking along a line where several horizontal members were joined to a vertical spine. The report notes that the joints themselves are intact and that the cracks run in the plate between welds. The steel was never painted and is ordinary mild plate.

questions.stem: The report records cracks running in the plate while the welds stay intact. What does that pattern tell the survey team?

options.text: That the welds were made with the wrong filler metal, since a bad weld would crack along its seam
options.misconception: blames the filler metal for cracks away from the seam

options.text: That the members have moved against one another and the plate absorbed the strain at its weakest section
That the steel plate was corroded by rain before the cracks appeared, since mild steel corrodes quickly
options.misconception: assumes rain corrosion preceded the cracking

options.text: That the vertical spine is too heavy for the members it carries, so the steel has slumped downward
options.misconception: invents a load failure without any evidence

questions.explanation: Cracks in the plate while the welds stay intact indicate movement rather than a failed joint, since a bad weld fails at the seam. A welded frame moves at its joints and the plate takes the strain.
questions.hint: Ask where a bad weld would have failed.

options.misconception: credits the rejected status of the objects

options.text: The eye level mounting places ordinary objects in a context reserved for precious things
options.misconception: credits the mounting height as the source of meaning

options.text: The chosen arrangement sets the relationships between the objects and gives the group its meaning
The number of objects, since a group of four reads differently from a single discarded tool
options.misconception: credits the count of objects rather than their arrangement

questions.explanation: Assemblage produces meaning through relations the maker sets, so the objects say something together that none says alone. Height and number may colour the reading, but arrangement carries it.

options.misconception: reduces the difference to a matter of date

options.text: Its materials are lighter, so it can be moved by a turning mechanism and therefore behaves differently
options.misconception: explains the difference through weight and mechanism

questions.learningObjective: Convert a model measurement into the full size span it represents
questions.stem: A model is built at 1 to 50 and its main span measures 0.6 metres. What full size span does the model represent?

options.text: 0.012 metres, since the scale reduces every measurement by a factor of 50
options.misconception: applies the scale factor in the wrong direction

options.text: 30 metres, since a scale of 1 to 50 means the model is one fiftieth of the real thing
50 metres, since the scale factor is the number of times the real work exceeds the model
options.misconception: confuses the scale factor with the resulting span

options.text: 3 metres, since the span is the model measurement divided by ten rather than multiplied
options.misconception: invents a tenfold reduction instead of the stated scale

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Installation and its dependence on site
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a calibrated installation loses meaning in a new place
questions.stem: An installation is built from the proportions of a courtyard: the arcade sets its scale and the paving sets its facing. Explain why it loses meaning when moved to a gallery.

answer.exemplar: The installation is calibrated to the place it was made for, and the calibration runs through scale, direction, light and sound. The height of the arcade sets the size of the standing figures, the angle of the paving sets the way they face, and the acoustics of the enclosed space govern how the sound moves through the work. In a gallery those relations cannot be supplied, so the same objects arrive without the setting that made them speak, and the result is a set of parts rather than the work they formed.

questions.explanation: When an installation is calibrated to the size, geometry and sound of a place, moving it destroys those calibrations. The objects remain, but the work they formed does not.
questions.hint: Ask what calibrations the site supplied.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a scale model can claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a scale model cannot demonstrate about weathering
questions.stem: A surveyor explains why a scale model of a building cannot settle questions of weathering. Explain the limit of what the model can demonstrate.

answer.exemplar: A model reproduces proportion and arrangement faithfully because those are scaled properties, so it can settle questions of mass, sightline and relationship. Weathering is not a scaled property at all, since a stone surface dulls, lichens and stains according to its own porosity and the number of seasons it has stood in a particular weather. A model made last week has had no life in the rain, so it cannot offer evidence about a century of exposure.

questions.explanation: Proportion and arrangement scale faithfully, which is why a model is good evidence about them. Weathering is not scaled but slow and material specific, so a recent model cannot testify to it.
questions.hint: Ask which properties actually scale.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of an occupied area taken by the work

questions.explanation: The log shows the alloy with more tin is harder but corrodes more readily, matching the behaviour of tin added to copper: strength rises while the protective qualities of pure copper fall away.

options.misconception: invents a requirement for annual repainting

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a kinetic construction different in kind
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a kinetic work is described as being in time
questions.stem: A guide explains why a kinetic work is often described as a work in time rather than a work in space. Explain what that description means.

answer.exemplar: A fixed sculpture has an identity that is complete at any instant, so a visitor can walk around it and still be looking at the same object. A kinetic work has no such instant: its panels are caught mid rotation, its balance is always changing and the sequence it performs is part of what it is. The work therefore occupies a span of time as thoroughly as it occupies a volume, and it can only be judged by what it does over that span rather than by what a photograph happens to catch.

questions.explanation: A kinetic work is only ever caught at a moment, so its identity lies in the sequence it performs rather than a single fixed appearance. Judging it from one instant is like judging music from one note.
questions.hint: Ask what a single photograph captures.

questions.topic: Assemblage and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Explain how arrangement alone can carry an argument
questions.stem: A curator asks how a collector's arrangement of unrelated objects can argue a point. Explain the mechanism that makes this possible.

answer.exemplar: When unrelated things are placed in a deliberate order, the viewer is invited to read a relation between them that was not there before the arrangement. A hinge, a float and a length of pipe say nothing to each other on their own, but set beside one another they begin to suggest a story about use, labour and disposal. The maker supplies the juxtaposition, and the argument is carried by the relation rather than by any single object.

questions.explanation: Placement creates relations that do not exist in the objects themselves, and those relations carry the reading. Nothing argues anything until the maker's ordering sets the things beside one another.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrangement adds to the objects.

questions.topic: The structural logic of a welded sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a visible weld contributes to a welded work
questions.stem: A foundry worker explains why the joints in a welded sculpture are usually left visible rather than polished away. Explain what the visible joint contributes.

answer.exemplar: A weld is a structural connection, and leaving it visible keeps the logic of the construction in the object rather than hiding it. The bead or the seam shows where one member was joined to another, so the viewer can read the sculpture as a structure that was put together from parts. Polishing the joints away would leave a continuous skin that hides how the thing is held up, and with it the reasoning that holds the whole form in the air.

questions.explanation: Visible joints keep the construction legible and let the viewer read the work as a structure assembled from members. Polishing them away hides how the form is held up.
questions.hint: Ask what the viewer learns from a visible seam.

questions.topic: What produces the colour of a patina
questions.learningObjective: Explain why patina is conserved as evidence
questions.stem: A field conservator explains why the patina on a bronze is protected as a surface in its own right. Explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: A patina is not simply a dull coating but a record of where the object has been and what it has met, and much of its character is created by the salts and pollutants of its surroundings. Once it has been scrubbed back to bright metal that evidence is gone and cannot be replaced, since the exposure that made the film cannot be repeated on demand. Conservators therefore treat the patina as part of the object's biography rather than as dirt to be removed.

questions.explanation: Patina records the object environment and age, and once cleaned away it cannot be restored, so conserving it preserves evidence. It is neither structural nor a carrier of the maker touch.
questions.hint: Ask what is lost if the surface is cleaned.

options.misconception: ties the model's value to the maker's identity

options.text: A model is entirely without authority, since only the finished work can be judged at all
options.misconception: denies the model any value whatever

options.text: A model is superior to the real work, since a reduced copy can be examined more closely and understood better
options.misconception: claims the model outranks the finished work

options.text: A model argues about arrangement and proportion, but cannot carry the mass or presence of the real work

questions.explanation: A scale model supports judgements about arrangement, proportion and sightlines, because those scale faithfully. It cannot evidence mass or presence, so its authority is partial and must be stated.
questions.hint: Ask what a reduced copy can still prove.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Installation and its dependence on site
questions.learningObjective: Interpret differing visitor responses to two sittings of one work
questions.stem: Two installations of the same objects are compared: in a bright open pavilion 22 percent of visitors paused, and in a dim enclosed room 61 percent paused. What is the defensible conclusion?

options.text: That the pavilion should be abandoned, since the work needs the enclosed room to be appreciated
options.misconception: advances abandoning the site on numbers alone

options.text: That the light and enclosure affect how visitors meet the work, so the setting is part of the encounter
That the visitors in the pavilion were mostly school groups and therefore counted unfairly
options.misconception: invents a demographic explanation for the counts

options.text: That the work should be moved indoors permanently, since indoor display always produces better attention
options.misconception: generalises from one comparison into a rule

questions.explanation: The same objects held attention far better in one setting, which shows that light, enclosure and distance shape the encounter. That is a fact about these two conditions, not a general rule.
questions.hint: Ask what else differed between the two rooms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What bronze's alloying contributes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bronze suits a bell hung outdoors
questions.stem: A surveyor explains why bronze was preferred to copper for a bell hung outdoors. Explain what the alloying changes about the metal's behaviour.

answer.exemplar: Copper alone is soft and easily deformed, but it resists corrosion reasonably well. Adding tin changes the first property decisively: the alloy is several times stiffer and harder, so a bell wall can be thin enough to ring yet stiff enough to keep its shape while swinging in the wind. The addition costs something in corrosion resistance, and the gain in stiffness is what a suspended bell depends on.

questions.explanation: Tin makes the alloy markedly stiffer and harder than copper, letting a bell wall be thin enough to ring yet stiff enough to hold its shape. The trade is some loss of corrosion resistance.
questions.hint: Ask what a swinging bell needs from its metal.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What produces the colour of a patina
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the remaining weight of a patinated object after loss
questions.stem: A patinated bronze cup loses 0.5 grams of metal each year on average. Starting at 820 grams, what will it weigh after 8 years if the loss is constant?
questions.explanation: The annual loss over eight years is 0.5 times 8, which is 4 grams. Subtracting that from the starting weight of 820 grams gives 816 grams for the cup.
questions.hint: Subtract the total loss from the starting weight.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural logic of a welded sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Locate the source of a failure in a welded structure

stimulus.body: A welded steel frame standing six metres high on a concrete base was found leaning after a storm. The notes record that the welds at the base were examined and found intact, with no cracking in the steel, and that a plinth at the foot of the base had shifted.

questions.stem: The welds are intact and the plinth has shifted. What does the leaning frame suggest about the cause?

options.text: That the storm moved the whole frame bodily, so the base must have failed in tension
options.misconception: claims the base failed in tension rather than at the joint

options.text: That the welds are sound but the steel is too soft, since only a softer metal could bend
options.misconception: blames the steel's softness rather than the footing

options.text: That the failure occurred in the base rather than in the welded frame, since the joints did not fail
That the frame was designed to lean, and the storm simply revealed the intended behaviour
options.misconception: invents a designed lean that the survey does not record

questions.explanation: The welds held, so the frame's structure survived and the movement came from below, in the base or its fixings. That is a question for the foundation, and the metal's strength is not in question.
questions.hint: Ask where the failure did not happen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Assemblage and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Identify the kind of work made from unaltered found objects
questions.stem: Stage one: the station acquires a broken clock mechanism and a length of rusted chain. Stage two: the display is closed and the objects are left in their found condition with only a descriptive label. What kind of work has been made?

options.text: A still life, since the display is a painted arrangement of objects on a table
options.misconception: calls the display a painted still life

options.text: A restoration, since the objects have been preserved and labelled for the public to see
options.misconception: treats conservation and labelling as restoration

options.text: A fabrication, since the display has been manufactured by the survey team from new parts
options.misconception: claims the team manufactured new parts for the display

options.text: An assemblage that argues through the chosen objects and their arrangement, not through altering them

questions.explanation: Objects brought together and left as found, with meaning carried by selection and arrangement rather than modification, constitute an assemblage. Labelling is care, not restoration.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything was made new or altered.
